title: Promises Made to God
overview: This chapter sets rules for vows made to God: a man must keep his, while a woman's vow could, in some situations, be cancelled by her father or husband.

parts.label: Keep your word (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: A vow was a voluntary promise to God spoken out loud, such as an extra offering or a time of fasting, and once said it had to be kept in full. Breaking it was treated as making your word worthless before God.

parts.label: A daughter at home (vv. 3-5)
parts.note: If a young unmarried woman made a vow, her father could cancel it on the day he heard of it, and if he stayed silent it stood. If he cancelled it, the LORD released her, so she carried no guilt for not keeping it.

parts.label: A woman who marries (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: If she married while a vow was still on her, even a hasty one, her new husband got the same single chance to cancel it when he learned of it. This seems meant to settle whose authority applied when she moved from her father's household to her husband's.

parts.label: Widows and divorced women (v. 9)
parts.note: A woman with no husband answered for her own vows, and they bound her just as a man's bound him. Even if she returned to her father's house, he could not cancel them.

parts.label: A wife's vows (vv. 10-15)
parts.note: A husband could confirm or cancel his wife's vows, including vows to deny herself, which probably means fasting, but silence for a day confirmed them. If he cancelled a vow later, the guilt for breaking it fell on him rather than on her.

parts.label: Summing up (v. 16)
parts.note: These rules reflect an ancient household where a woman lived under the authority of a father or husband, which limited her freedom to make religious commitments on her own. At the same time, they shielded her from blame when a man overruled her.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the authority given here to fathers and husbands is a lasting pattern for families or a feature of ancient Israelite household law that later teaching moved beyond.
think: What makes a promise feel truly binding to you, and should anyone else ever have the power to release you from one?
